## Integral Equality

### Problem
Let $f$ be a function continuous on $[0, \pi]$. Show that

$$\int_0^\pi x f(\sin x) \, dx = \frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) \, dx.$$

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
Let $I = \int_0^\pi x f(\sin x) \, dx$.

Apply the substitution $u = \pi - x$, so $dx = -du$.
When $x = 0$, $u = \pi$; when $x = \pi$, $u = 0$.
Since $\sin(\pi - u) = \sin u$, we have:

$$\begin{aligned} I &= \int_\pi^0 (\pi - u) f(\sin(\pi - u)) (-du) \\ &= \int_0^\pi (\pi - u) f(\sin u) \, du \\ &= \pi \int_0^\pi f(\sin u) \, du - \int_0^\pi u f(\sin u) \, du \\ &= \pi \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) \, dx - I. \end{aligned}$$

Adding $I$ to both sides:

$$2I = \pi \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) \, dx.$$

Dividing by 2:

$$I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) \, dx.$$

### Conceptual Explanation
Applying King's property / reflection substitution $u = \pi - x$ exploits the symmetry $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$, giving $I = \pi \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) dx - I$, whence $2I = \pi \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) dx$.

### Key Technique
King's property $\int_a^b g(x) dx = \int_a^b g(a+b-x) dx$ with trigonometric reflection $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$.
